title: Linear-time rule mining under formal guarantees
claim: A small relational datagraph of entities and typed edges illustrates the data that logical rules are mined from.
layout: single panel, triangle of three nodes, edge labels along lines, one red edge
description: A single minimal black-and-white graph drawn as a triangle. Three circular nodes carry the lowercase labels s at the top, a at bottom left, and b at bottom right. Straight lines connect them. The two slanted lines from s to a and from s to b are black and labeled LIKES in serif capitals, rotated to follow each line. The horizontal line between a and b is red and labeled FRIENDS. The red edge is the only color and draws the eye first. The figure shows a toy relational database as a datagraph, with entities as nodes and relations as labeled edges. It sets up a running example of the pattern that LIKES edges to a shared entity imply FRIENDS, which a mined rule could capture. There are no arrows, legends or other annotations.
caption: Datagraph GD for D in Example 3.1.
abstract: Probabilistic logical models are a core component of neurosymbolic AI and are important in their own right for tasks that require high explainability. Unlike neural networks, logical theories that underlie the model are often handcrafted using domain expertise, making their development costly and prone to errors. While there are algorithms that learn logical theories from data, they are generally prohibitively expensive, limiting their applicability in real-world settings. Here, we introduce precision and recall for logical rules and define their composition as rule utility -- a measure of the predictive power of logical theories that can be computed in linear time in the data size. We then present SPECTRUM, a linear-time framework for learning logical theories from relational data, that mines recurrent patterns in the data, and subsequently uses our utility measure to evaluate and rank the rules derived from these patterns. Finally, we prove theoretical guarantees on the utility of the learnt logical theory. As a result, we demonstrate across various tasks that SPECTRUM scales to databases with orders of magnitude more relations and entities, often learning more accurate logical theories on CPUs in < 1% of the runtime of state-of-the-art neural network approaches on GPUs.
